prompt:
Use case: illustration-story. Create one realistic cinematic historical/literary illustration for Joel 1:7–12, landscape 3:2, requested 1536x1024.

Main subject: one adult farmer or vinedresser in plain ancient Levantine work clothes, clearly visible at left foreground, mourning the ruined harvest. He stands beside a stripped grapevine and a fig tree with barked white branches, looking at the bare crop with a hand resting on the vine. A small, readable locust swarm crosses the left half of the image and gathers on damaged plants. Show dried grain stalks, vine and fig, not a battle. The farmer is the subject; do not make this an empty landscape.

Composition: keep the farmer, damaged vines and trees, and all visible locusts left of x=62%. Farmer around x=24%; vines and fig tree around x=40–55%. Reserve the entire right 38% as low-detail dry field and muted sky for reader overlay. Top and bottom 12% noncritical. One continuous scene, no montage.

Setting and mood: generic ancient agricultural hillside, no identifiable location, no ruins or buildings. Sunlit but subdued, with warm ochre, dusty olive, pale bark, faded grape leaves and cream cloth. Realistic cinematic historical/literary painting matching the supplied Bible illustration references; tactile woven cloth, bark, dry soil. Mournful without sensationalism.
Interpretation: Joel's poem describes successive locusts and widespread agricultural loss, then uses national language in the same oracle. Show locusts and crop damage as the poem's imagery; do not label them as a specific army, invasion, or archaeologically documented event. Do not add religious iconography or depict God/LORD in human form.
Avoid: text, letters, captions, labels, verse numbers, pins, UI, logos, watermark, maps, modern objects, recognizable monuments, weapons, soldiers, fires, corpses, fantasy, empty landform diorama, too many insects obscuring the farmer, and any person or dense crop detail in the right third.
notes: Final raster reviewed against the named subjects; account-specific references remain in the scene registry. Historical appearances are reconstructed and literary scenes are labeled.
